title: The Happy Prince and Other Tales
author: Oscar Wilde
short_summary: This 1888 collection gathers five of Oscar Wilde's fairy tales: 'The Happy Prince', 'The Nightingale and the Rose', 'The Selfish Giant', 'The Devoted Friend' and 'The Remarkable Rocket'. A gilded statue gives itself away piece by piece, a bird dies to make one red rose, a giant pulls down his own wall, a miller talks about friendship while using a friend up, and a firework believes the world is watching him. Wilde's beauty always costs somebody something.
extended_summary:
In 'The Happy Prince' a gilded statue with sapphire eyes persuades a swallow to carry away his jewels and gold to the poor of the city, until he is grey and blind and the bird is dead of cold; the two of them are thrown out as rubbish, and then chosen as the two most precious things in the city. In 'The Nightingale and the Rose' a student needs a red rose to win a dance; a nightingale presses her breast to a thorn and sings all night to make one — and the girl throws it away, because someone else has sent her jewels.

'The Selfish Giant' walls off his garden and is punished with a winter that will not end, until the children creep back through a gap and spring comes with them; years later the smallest child returns with wounds in his hands and feet and takes the Giant with him. In 'The Devoted Friend', a miller talks endlessly about friendship while working little Hans to death and never handing over the broken wheelbarrow he has promised. And in 'The Remarkable Rocket', a firework so impressed with himself that he weeps and gets damp finally goes off in broad daylight with nobody there to see it, convinced he has caused a sensation.

The five tales are short, funny and cruel in different proportions. In every one of them somebody gives something away entirely, and somebody else fails to notice.

questions.prompt: In 'The Nightingale and the Rose', how does the nightingale make a red rose grow?

options: She sings all night with a thorn in her breast
She waters the bush with her own tears
She carries red petals from the king's garden
She begs the Tree to bloom out of season

questions.explanation: The white rose tree tells her the only way: press against a thorn and sing until the thorn reaches her heart. She does it, the rose turns red as it drinks her blood, and the whole thing is done for a student she has decided must be a true lover.

questions.prompt: The student takes the red rose to the professor's daughter. What happens to it?

options: She refuses it, and he throws it into the gutter
She wears it, and they dance together all evening
She presses it in a book and forgets about it
He loses it in the street on the way to the house

questions.explanation: The girl points out that another suitor has sent her real jewels, and that flowers cost nothing. The student throws the rose into the road, a cart-wheel goes over it, and he decides love is a silly thing and goes back to his books. The nightingale's death is never noticed by anyone.

questions.prompt: The Selfish Giant builds a high wall around his garden and puts up a notice board: "TRESPASSERS WILL BE ___."
questions.explanation: It is the only notice board in the collection, and Wilde puts it in capitals for a reason. The Giant has done nothing violent — he has simply asserted, in the most ordinary legal language, that the garden is his. Winter arrives the same week.

questions.prompt: The Giant's garden stays frozen while the rest of the country has spring. What finally brings spring back?

options: The children creep in through a gap in the wall
The Giant apologises to the Snow and the Frost
The Giant plants new trees to replace the old
A warm wind blows over the wall from the south

questions.explanation: Spring in this story is not weather; it is the children. Where they are, the trees blossom, and where they are shut out, it snows in July. The Giant works this out by looking out of his window one morning — and immediately takes an axe to his own wall.

questions.prompt: Put the events of 'The Devoted Friend' in the order they happen.

items: The Miller promises little Hans his broken wheelbarrow
Hans gives away his flowers and his plank of wood
Hans works through the spring instead of his own garden
The Miller sends Hans out at night to fetch the doctor
Hans loses his way on the moor and drowns
The Miller complains at the funeral about the wheelbarrow

questions.explanation: The wheelbarrow is never actually given. Every demand the Miller makes is justified by that promise, and at the funeral he is still annoyed — now he is stuck with a barrow nobody will take off his hands. Wilde lets him say it out loud, and says nothing himself.

questions.prompt: Match each detail to the tale it belongs to.

left: A swallow on its way to Egypt
A thorn pressed into a breast
A damp firework in a ditch

questions.explanation: Four objects, four tales, and the same pattern in each: something small and ordinary carries the whole weight of the story. Wilde never explains his symbols — he just puts a wheelbarrow in the middle of a friendship and lets you watch.

questions.prompt: Sort each detail into the tale it comes from.

options.label: A high wall goes up around a garden
Snow and Frost move in and stay for years
A small boy is lifted into a tree
A promise about a wheelbarrow is never kept
A friend is sent out in a storm at night
The chief mourner complains at a funeral

questions.explanation: Both tales are about a person who believes he has done nothing wrong. The Giant finds out and knocks down his wall; the Miller never finds out at all, and Wilde leaves him exactly as he was. It is the same story told twice, once with mercy and once without.

questions.prompt: In 'The Remarkable Rocket', what is the joke of the ending?

options: He goes off unseen and thinks he has caused a sensation
He is set off at the wedding after all and disappoints
He is stolen by a boy who sells him in the market
He explains himself so long that the fireworks end

questions.explanation: He goes off in broad daylight, in an empty field; the only witnesses are a goose and two boys who do not look up. His stick falls on the goose, and he dies convinced he has created a magnificent effect. Wilde's joke is that nothing at all has changed his opinion of himself.

questions.prompt: The Miller talks constantly about friendship, and little Hans gives him flowers, wood, work and finally his life. Was Hans a good friend, or was he simply being used and should have said no? Give your reasons.
questions.explanation: Both positions can earn full marks. A strong 'he was a good friend' answer notices that Hans gives gladly and that the story's contempt is aimed entirely at the Miller, not at him. A strong 'he was being used' answer notices that the wheelbarrow never arrives, that the demands grow, and that Hans dies on an errand he should have refused. Accept either, argued from the tale.

questions.prompt: In these tales, somebody usually gives everything away and somebody else never notices. Invent the opening of a new Wilde tale in the same shape: who gives, what do they give up, and who fails to notice?
questions.explanation: There is no single right answer. A strong answer has all three parts — a giver, a real cost, and someone who does not see it — because that triangle is the pattern of every tale in the book. A story where the giver is thanked and rewarded has copied the shape of a different kind of fairy tale.

questions.prompt: In 'The Happy Prince', the statue's eyes are two bright ___, which he asks the swallow to pluck out and carry away.
questions.explanation: He gives away the ruby from his sword-hilt first, then the two sapphires, then the gold leaf from his body. Each gift costs him a sense or a surface: by the end he is blind, grey and entirely unbeautiful — which is the point.

questions.prompt: At the end of 'The Happy Prince', which two things are chosen as the most precious in the whole city?

options: The cracked lead heart and the dead swallow
The ruby and the two sapphire eyes
The gold leaf and the statue's sword
The town councillors' own memorial

questions.explanation: The furnace will not melt the broken lead heart, and it is thrown on a dust heap beside the dead bird. Those are the two objects called for — the only things in the story that were given rather than owned.
